clue.text: Yankee in a story of a dystopian future — a male historical novelist called Stanley

indicators.note: Yankee goes in, placed between the two pieces that make the rest of the name

parts.words: a story of a dystopian future
parts.note: We is Yevgeny Zamyatin's dystopian novel
Yankee is Y in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A muddled literary list: an American in a dystopian tale, a man, and a historical novelist named Stanley.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'story of a dystopian future' is Zamyatin's 1920s Russian novel We, a model for Orwell's 1984.
explanation.definitionFit: Stanley Weyman wrote swashbuckling historical romances such as A Gentleman of France.

clue.text: Maiden pursuing promotion parts with Mary, who looks after two children in Baltimore

definitions.text: Mary, who looks after two children in Baltimore

indicators.note: parts is read as a verb: the word with is split apart to take something in
pursuing means coming after, so the maiden's letter follows the promotion

parts.note: M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: A girl chasing advancement leaves a woman who minds two children in Baltimore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'parts' is a verb here, not a noun. Mary Wadsmith is a character in one of Anne Tyler's Baltimore novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary Wadsmith is the fictional carer of two children in an Anne Tyler novel set in Baltimore.

clue.text: Long time on farmland made a former agricultural worker a poet

parts.note: a long time can be years
a ley is land temporarily put down to grass

explanation.surface: Time spent working the fields turned a farm labourer into a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Ann Yearsley was the eighteenth-century Bristol milkwoman poet known as Lactilla; 'made ... a poet' completes the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Ann Yearsley sold milk door to door, a dairy labourer before her verse made her famous.

clue.text: A famous orphan found in a basket

definitions.text: A famous orphan found in a basket

parts.words: A famous orphan found in a basket
parts.note: the red-haired heroine of the comic strip and Broadway musical, left as a baby on the orphanage doorstep in a basket

explanation.definitionFit: Little Orphan Annie, of the comic strip and musical, was a foundling left at an orphanage.

clue.text: Term for someone who isn't English — Welsh perhaps

definitions.text: Term for someone who isn't English
definitions.meaning: a native of Scotland is one kind of Briton who is not English
Irvine Welsh, author of Trainspotting, is a Scot from Edinburgh

explanation.surface: A description of a non-English Briton, offering Welsh as the example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Welsh' seems to name a nationality but is the novelist Irvine Welsh, born in Leith.
explanation.definitionFit: A man born in Scotland is British but not English; Irvine Welsh is one such man.

clue.text: Feminist author's mildness mostly to chap involved in drugs

definitions.note: the 's stands for is, joining the definition to the wordplay

indicators.note: mostly means nearly all, so the final letter of the word is dropped
the chap is involved in, set inside, the two drug letters

parts.note: E for ecstasy, twice for plural drugs

explanation.surface: A feminist writer is gentle, more or less, towards a man caught up with drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: Plural 'drugs' gives two ecstasy letters around the chap. Clemence Dane was the pen name of Winifred Ashton.
explanation.definitionFit: Clemence Dane, dramatist and novelist, wrote on women's education and careers, earning the feminist label.

clue.text: Burns production in dilapidated silo with torch

indicators.note: something dilapidated has fallen apart, so these letters are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: A fire in a run-down grain store set off with a torch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Burns' looks like fire, matching 'torch', but it is Robert Burns; his song To Chloris is the production.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Burns wrote several lyrics addressed to Chloris, his name for Jean Lorimer.

clue.text: Monsieur, solitary character created by someone who often wrote in French

definitions.text: character created by someone who often wrote in French

explanation.surface: A lonely Frenchman, a figure invented by a writer who worked in French.
explanation.walkthrough: Malone is Samuel Beckett's dying narrator in Malone Dies, first written in French.
explanation.definitionFit: Malone is the bedridden protagonist of Beckett's novel Malone meurt, which he wrote in French.

clue.text: Poet from Nebraska, comparatively coarse in speech

parts.note: NE is the postal abbreviation for Nebraska

indicators.note: in speech says the word for coarser is said aloud, not spelt

explanation.surface: A Midwestern poet, somewhat cruder in how he talks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in speech' tells you RUDER is heard, in a non-rhotic British accent, as RUDA. Pablo Neruda was Chilean, not from Nebraska.
explanation.definitionFit: Pablo Neruda, the Chilean Nobel laureate, wrote Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair.

clue.text: "Hide me from the hostile light (…) / That — the blood of suffering men" (Charlotte Brontë)

definitions.text: "Hide me from the hostile light (…) / That — the blood of suffering men" (Charlotte Brontë)

parts.words: "Hide me from the hostile light (…) / That — the blood of suffering men" (Charlotte Brontë)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap: the missing verb says what the hostile light does to the blood of suffering men

explanation.definitionFit: The light empties out the sufferers' blood, as a sink takes water away.

clue.text: Lad working with scree — that's supposed to remove unwanted mineral deposits

definitions.text: that's supposed to remove unwanted mineral deposits

indicators.note: working here means being worked over, so the letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: A boy toiling on a loose rock slope, with a product that should strip limescale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'working' signals the anagram of LAD + SCREE.
explanation.definitionFit: A kettle or boiler cleaner dissolves limescale, the chalky deposit hard water leaves.

clue.text: Bishop in calamitous battle with Satan, an evil creature in epic poetry

definitions.text: an evil creature in epic poetry

indicators.note: the bishop goes in, placed inside the rearranged letters
calamitous suggests disaster, so these letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A churchman caught in a disastrous fight against the Devil, a monster of epic verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'calamitous' rearranges the two words into BLATANTEAST, and the bishop slips in. The Blatant Beast is the slander monster of Spenser's The Faerie Queene.
explanation.definitionFit: Spenser's thousand-tongued monster symbolising slander roams Book VI of The Faerie Queene.

clue.text: Pirate leader unexpectedly seems to protect one with shelter

indicators.note: the shuffled letters protect, surround, the letter for one
unexpectedly means the letters turn up in a surprising order

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
lee is shelter from the wind

explanation.surface: A buccaneer captain surprisingly appears to shield someone with cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unexpectedly' gives MSSEE, which takes the I inside. Miss Ee Lee is the pirate chief in Arthur Ransome's Missee Lee.
explanation.definitionFit: In Arthur Ransome's novel the Cambridge-educated Miss Lee commands a fleet of Chinese pirates.

clue.text: Like some pages of narrative beginning and ending in cover

indicators.note: the outside letters go in, placed inside the word for a cover
beginning and ending picks the first and last letters of narrative

explanation.surface: Pages of a story, opening and closing inside a book jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning and ending' takes N and E from narrative; 'in' places them in LID.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing paper with ruled rules across it, as in exercise books, has horizontal guides printed on it.

clue.text: Work based in Deptford, with subject matter including one fooling around with men

indicators.note: including means the word for subject matter holds the other pieces inside it

parts.note: an antic is a clown or buffoon
OR, other ranks, means ordinary soldiers, men

explanation.surface: A book set in a London district whose theme is a joker playing about with men.
explanation.walkthrough: Deptford is not the London district but the Ontario village of Robertson Davies's Deptford Trilogy, whose second novel this is.
explanation.definitionFit: The Manticore (1972) is the middle novel of Robertson Davies's Deptford Trilogy.

clue.text: Female novelist, rejected in a meeting with a TLS crossword setter? There's nothing in it

indicators.note: rejected means turned back, so these words are read backwards
in it says the nothing goes inside the setter's name

parts.note: TLS setters take names from Greek myth, and Talos is one of them

explanation.surface: A woman writer snubbed at a meeting with a puzzle setter who finds nothing in the clue.
explanation.walkthrough: TLS setters, this one Broteas included, use names from Greek myth. Anita Loos wrote Gentlemen Prefer Blondes.
explanation.definitionFit: Anita Loos was the American writer of the comic novel Gentlemen Prefer Blondes.

clue.text: Tales about Ena and Ethel's admirer

indicators.note: about means moved around, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Stories concerning two women, Ena and Ethel, and an admirer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges TALES. Mr Salteena courts Ethel Monticue in Daisy Ashford's The Young Visiters.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Young Visiters, written by nine-year-old Daisy Ashford, Mr Salteena loves Ethel.

clue.text: American sci-fi writer's country girl Kate, concealing mounting difficulty

definitions.note: the 's stands for is, joining the definition to the wordplay

indicators.note: concealing means the surname wraps round another piece

parts.note: Kate Brady is a heroine of Edna O'Brien's The Country Girls

indicators.note: mounting means going up, so in a down clue the word is read upwards

parts.note: a rub is a difficulty, as in there's the rub

explanation.surface: A US science-fiction author's rural heroine hiding a growing problem.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'mounting' reads upwards. Ray Bradbury wrote Fahrenheit 451.
explanation.definitionFit: Ray Bradbury wrote The Martian Chronicles and Fahrenheit 451.

clue.text: Savage castle owner, a chap protected by two soldiers and another two on his other side

indicators.note: protected by means the chap stands guarded with pieces on both sides of him
on his other side means the second pair comes after the chap

parts.note: a GI is an American soldier
a soldier ant is a warrior caste, so ant is a soldier

explanation.surface: A brutal lord of a castle, a man flanked by two soldiers with two more beyond him.
explanation.walkthrough: Soldier ants are a crossword staple. Giant Despair of Doubting Castle is in Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress.
explanation.definitionFit: In Bunyan's allegory, the cruel giant imprisons and beats Christian and Hopeful in Doubting Castle.

clue.text: Lots of poetry is tricky to scan

indicators.note: tricky suggests the letters are slippery and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: Plenty of verse is hard to scan metrically.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tricky' rearranges TO SCAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Long poems such as Pound's or Dante's are divided into many sections.

clue.text: Scott's noble lady artist welcomes a humble philanthropist

indicators.note: welcomes means takes in, so the artist's letters surround the other piece

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, an artist
Robert Owen, of humble Welsh birth, was the philanthropic mill reformer of New Lanark

explanation.surface: A Walter Scott heroine, painter, receives a modest benefactor.
explanation.walkthrough: RA, Royal Academician, is the usual crossword artist. Rowena is the Saxon heiress in Scott's Ivanhoe.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Rowena is the Saxon noblewoman Ivanhoe marries in Scott's novel.

clue.text: Part of Pythagoras' milieu?

indicators.note: part of says the letters are found inside the philosopher's name

explanation.surface: A question about the world the Greek mathematician lived and worked in.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits inside Pythagoras' name, and the whole clue describes a Greek public square he would have known.
explanation.definitionFit: An ancient Greek city's marketplace and public meeting ground was where philosophers held forth.

clue.text: Priestley novel with a plot capturing English darkness

indicators.note: capturing means the plot holds the other letters inside it

parts.note: a bed is a garden plot

explanation.surface: A J.B. Priestley book, its storyline gripping English gloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plot' looks like a storyline but is a flower bed. Benighted (1927) is Priestley's novel filmed as The Old Dark House.
explanation.definitionFit: J.B. Priestley's 1927 novel Benighted is about travellers stranded in a sinister Welsh house.

clue.text: Longstanding noble family's complaint

definitions.meaning: the ancient aristocratic house of Gormenghast in Mervyn Peake's novels; 's here stands for is
a complaint is a moan of displeasure

explanation.surface: An old aristocratic family's grievance.
explanation.walkthrough: The family is Mervyn Peake's, rulers of Gormenghast in Titus Groan.
explanation.definitionFit: Peake's Titus is the 77th Earl of Gormenghast; a moan of displeasure is a sound of complaint.

clue.text: Spanish article found in a chest is a fabulous book about environmental issues

definitions.text: a fabulous book about environmental issues

indicators.note: found in means the article sits inside the word for chest

explanation.surface: A Spanish word turns up in a box, a fable about saving nature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chest' looks like a box but is the body part. Dr Seuss's The Lorax is a parable about deforestation.
explanation.definitionFit: Dr Seuss's picture-book fable has a creature speaking for the trees against industrial greed.

clue.text: Doctor Auer, strange and sinister surgeon

parts.note: MO is a medical officer, a doctor

indicators.note: strange means the letters come out oddly arranged

explanation.surface: A Dr Auer described as weird and an evil surgeon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like part of a title, but gives MO; 'strange' rearranges AUER. Doctor Moreau is H.G. Wells's vivisectionist.
explanation.definitionFit: Wells's Doctor Moreau surgically turns animals into beast-men on his island.

clue.text: Rare quality of a place like Bath, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly says the phrase is heard, not spelt

parts.note: Bath, famous for its Roman baths, is a spa city

explanation.surface: An uncommon attribute of an English resort town, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rare' looks like 'precious', but means thinly spread. In a non-rhotic British accent SPA CITY sounds the same; Bath is a Somerset spa city.
explanation.definitionFit: Thinness of spread is the state of being scarce or uncommon.

clue.text: Scandal among footballers? Good heavens!

parts.note: the FA is the Football Association
my! is an exclamation of surprise

explanation.surface: A footballers' disgrace greeted with a shocked exclamation.
explanation.walkthrough: The FA, the Football Association, governs English football.
explanation.definitionFit: Disgrace and public notoriety from wrongdoing are what a scandal brings.
